1:
Adam Clarke opens with the authorship, never settled though the book was always received as canonical. It is generally given to Solomon; one critic put it long after him, a guess Clarke thinks ill-founded, while granting he was better on the language, showing many words that do not savour of the purity of Hebrew and belong to the captivity and after. A later examiner argued the same from its Chaldaisms and Hellenisms; reviewers made it a translation from the Greek by a Jew of Alexandria, written while the famous library was founded, referring the complaint that of making many books there is no end to that circumstance. Clarke reports that the Jews generally, and an early Latin father, hold it Solomon’s and the fruit of his repentance; others place it before his fall, since there is no evidence he wrote after it, or ever recovered. He presses the objection honestly, noting it goes far towards destroying the inspiration of the book: God appeared to him twice before the fall with no intimation of a third, and the history reports his wives turning away his heart and then his death, with no word of repentance. Yet none of this, he says, can affect the utility of a work of singular worth, the finest monument of ancient wisdom except one.

Matthew Henry reads the concealment of the name as confession: the man called peaceable had by his sin broken his peace with God and lost the peace of his conscience—call me not that, he says, but bitterness. On the title he follows the root meaning to gather, two ways at once. It is a penitent soul, one gathered, that had gone astray like a lost sheep and is now gathered home, its spirit dissipated after a thousand vanities collected again and made to centre in God; and a preaching soul, one gathering, drawing in others his example may have led astray, since a man who has done anything to seduce his brother should do all he can to restore him. Hence Henry’s two rules, that penitents should be preachers, and preachers preaching souls, for only what comes from the heart is likely to reach the heart. He turns the remaining titles the same way: sonship to a good father was an honour, an aggravation, and an encouragement, since that father had fallen and repented and found mercy; kingship aggravated the sin, his dignity making the example more dangerous in the holy city, while lending weight to what he writes, for where the word of a king is there is power. John Wesley puts it briefly: one who had sinned grievously in the eyes of all the world thought himself obliged to publish his repentance and warn others off the rocks on which he split.

Charles Ellicott prefers convener to preacher, notes the word takes a feminine termination in one place though elsewhere masculine, and compares other books opening with the same formula. John Gill stresses that the whole is one continued discourse of solid matter, not words only. Clarke adds that some read it as a dialogue between a believer and an unbeliever, which would explain its contradictions by assigning parts to speakers; he is not convinced, though he allows unbelieving opinions are sometimes quoted, and reproduces another scheme reducing the whole to three propositions, the first that no labour of man in this world can content him. Keil and Delitzsch set the book against the alternatives: the world without God is a graduated combination of causes and effects and calculated means and ends, yet as a whole a mystery, for to drop the idea of God abandons the question of origins, and to identify God with the world makes the effect one with its cause. The moral order presupposes an absolutely good Being and demands a Lawgiver and Judge; apart from him good and evil lose their depth and sharpness.
2:
All treat the opening cry as the thesis. John Gill calls it the preacher’s text, the theme he afterwards enlarges and proves by an induction of particulars. Keil and Delitzsch say the book begins artistically with a preamble in which the ground-tone sounds at once. Charles Ellicott presses it further: the unity of the book is that of a musical composition rather than a philosophical treatise, a leading theme given out and followed, episodes introduced that are not perhaps logically connected but treated in harmony with it and leading back, the theme never lost sight of and sounding again at the close. Adam Clarke would render it as the exclamation it is—O vanity of vanities, emptiness of emptinesses—since substantial good is not found in anything liable to change and corruption, and gives most of his space to a verse paraphrase likening the world’s largest gifts to painted clouds and watery bubbles, the human race dropping like autumnal leaves, mightiest realms sinking while new estates rise from their ruins, the earth itself coming at last to a period unknown to man.

On the word itself Ellicott is the most exact. It occurs thirty-seven times here and only thirty-three in all the rest of the older scriptures; its primary sense is breath or vapour, and some of the Greek versions render it so; it is the same word as a proper name in the first book, and is applied elsewhere to the follies of the heathen and to the estate of men. Doubling it is the ordinary Hebrew superlative, of a piece with heaven of heavens and song of songs. John Wesley reaches the same superlative by feel rather than grammar—not merely vain but vanity in the abstract, the vainest vanity, redoubled because the thing is certain beyond dispute—and enters the one qualification the others do not: worldly things are not vain in themselves, being creatures of God and good in their kinds, but only in reference to the happiness men expect from them, since they are not what they seem and do not perform what they promise, and become the occasion of innumerable cares and sorrows.

The verb of speaking divides the two closest readers. Keil and Delitzsch take it as present utterance rather than a saying recorded from the past, since it is those now living to whom this preacher, and through him the author, preaches the vanity of earthly things. Ellicott begins from the same ambiguity—Hebrew constantly uses the past where English needs the present, and in a message the point contemplated is the giving, not the delivery—but draws the opposite inference: the formula might conceivably be used by a man writing down his own words, yet it rather suggests we have them written down by another.

The question that follows is read by all as a denial in interrogative dress. Gill says it carries a strong negative, and takes labour widely, since everything a man enjoys is got by it—bread by the sweat of the brow as part of the curse, wealth by a diligent hand under a blessing, knowledge through much weariness of the flesh. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for profit belongs to this book alone and means what remains over, whether gain or precedence, and that the phrase under the sun is likewise its own, naming the world of men. Ellicott counts both and observes that other books say under heaven. Gill hears the phrase as measuring out the working day, the sun sending man out to his labour and lighting it, though in some climates its noon heat makes the labour burdensome; Wesley hears in the same restriction an implication, that the happiness sought in vain below is really to be found in heavenly things. Clarke asks what sum of real good the toils of a life have gained, and answers that in themselves they have made no man contented or happy.
4:
Matthew Henry makes the passing of generations the first proof. Our tenure is one generation, itself passing to make room for another, and we pass with it; our possessions we lately had from others and must shortly leave to others, and are no more substantial than the life that carries them, a vapour appearing for a little and vanishing. He puts it in a figure—while the stream of mankind flows on, how little enjoyment has one drop of it of the pleasant banks between which it glides—and draws a duty from the succession: to glorify God for his patience in continuing a sinful species and his power in continuing a dying one. John Wesley adds why happiness cannot lodge here: it must be unchangeable and eternal, or the knowledge that all will be lost robs a man of contentment in it. John Gill notes that a man leaves what he has almost as soon as he has got it, and that this holds of kingdoms as well as persons.

The permanence of the earth is contrast, not comfort. Wesley makes man more mutable than the ground he stands on; Henry that we leave the earth behind where it abides, so its things stand us in no stead hereafter, and that here our condition is worse than the creatures’—the sun sets but rises as fresh as ever, the winds shift their point but are always in some point, the sea’s waters come back under ground, but man lies down and rises not. Keil and Delitzsch are careful what the permanence proves: not that the earth approaches no limit, but that nothing here remains as the fixed point around which all circles, the earth being the standing scene of ceaseless change. Both things could be said of it, they allow—that it never loses its place, and that it will one day be changed into something else—but the second belongs to redemption history and is remote from this writer, for whom its stability is only the foil of a decay endlessly repeated.

On the sun the readings converge. Keil and Delitzsch note that its setting is no rest, since from its resting-place in the west it must rise in the east; Gill says it pants, as the word means, like a man out of breath with running, and takes the same track; Charles Ellicott confirms that verb, used of eager desire. Henry gathers them: all things are movable and mutable, constant in nothing but inconstancy, and but once did the sun stand still. Yet though everything moves, everything is where it was—and so is the man who took all these pains, still as far to seek as ever, his mind as restless as sun and wind and rivers and no better satisfied, no sooner filled than the sea by the rivers running into it. Wesley finds the weariness in the repetition, so irksome that the thought of it has made some men weary of their lives, the world being too narrow for a mind that must have something new. Keil and Delitzsch hear it in the prosody, the verse deliberately long-drawn and monotonous, to give an impression of weariness.

One disagreement is sharp. Adam Clarke holds that the clause about going south and circling north belongs to the sun and the previous verse, that all the versions so apply it and our English version alone has mistaken it; he cites an old manuscript Bible and reads it as the sun’s annual passage between the tropics. Gill agrees the word wind is absent from the original there and takes it of the sun, with the Targum. Ellicott concedes the word order permits it and that some have taken it so, but calls it probably erroneous, preferring a livelier rendering in which the wind circles and circles and returns upon its circles; Wesley simply reads the wind, blowing now from one quarter and now another.
7:
Why the sea never fills is answered several ways. John Gill canvasses the ancients: one wondered that the accession of rivers is not perceived in the sea, and accounted for it by the sun’s exhalations, by drying winds, and by what the clouds take up; one poet made every sea and fountain flow out of the main ocean, others had the rivers flowing into it as the wise man does. Gill concludes both may be true. Adam Clarke gives the circuit as physics: nothing enters the sea that did not come from it, the exhaled water collecting in cloud, falling on the mountain tops, filtering through their fissures into streams which unite into rivers. Keil and Delitzsch defend the statement as consistent with fact: the author does not mean that every river flows thither immediately, nor this or that sea, nor the earth as a ring encircling the ocean as one paraphrase has it, but the sea in general, perhaps including a hidden ocean—on which reckoning the rivers lost in deserts and closed lakes form no exception. Charles Ellicott reverses the last clause: whither the rivers go, not whence they come. John Wesley keeps the moral: the sea not overflowing intimates the emptiness of men’s minds for all their creature comforts.

The next verse turns on one word. Keil and Delitzsch reject the renderings that take it of words—that no speech could describe this sameness—since the verb denotes not what causes weariness but what suffers it, and to shift the affection from the narrator to the thing narrated would be too affected for a poet; they render, all things are in activity. Ellicott records the rival sense, that other instances might be mentioned but are too many to recount, and declines it. Gill takes the plain one: those who load themselves with thick clay weary themselves, crowns are weighty cares, and much study is a weariness to the flesh. Clarke says it is impossible to calculate the fatigue the common operations of life require, and that an endless desire of gain and an endless curiosity carry men through them. Wesley explains why these two senses are named: they stand for all, being the most refined and inquisitive, the most capable of satisfaction, and exercised with most ease.

Matthew Henry takes the denial of novelty as a rebuke to one vanity, the pleasure of thinking none ever made such advances as we, so that older contrivances are run down while we boast of new fashions, new hypotheses, new methods that jostle out the old. He challenges those who cry up modern learning above the ancients: name the thing that is new, and though we may not trace it for want of the records of former times, we have reason to conclude it has been already of old. Things that appear new to us, as they do to children, are not new in themselves; and in providence, which keeps no such fixed track as nature, it is still repetition. He quotes an ancient writer telling the Grecians not to call inventions what are only imitations. His three uses follow: that we nauseate old things and covet, like the Athenians, to hear some new thing; that we should stop expecting from the world what none before us got; and that whoever would be entertained with new things must get a new nature. Gill connects it to the unsatisfied senses, there being nothing else to see or hear. Clarke lists the revolutions of heat and cold, rain and drought, and denies anything absolutely new in sublunary things; Wesley infers that since no man ever received satisfaction from worldly things it is vain for any to expect it. Ellicott alone looks outward, setting against the verse the prophetic promises of a new thing, and noting that an early apologist seems to echo it, though the same idea in Greek philosophy makes the echo prove nothing.
10:
The challenge to name a new thing is read as an appeal to observation. John Gill invites the reader to test it in every field—in nature the same causes produce the same effects, in morals the same virtues and their contraries, in politics the same schemes ending in peace or war, in learning the same things said over again—though he allows the words may be a concession in the form of an objection. Adam Clarke renders it as though the thing itself were asked to speak: men may say this of their discoveries, but universal nature answers that it is not new. Keil and Delitzsch take the opening verb as a hypothetical antecedent, supposing there is such a thing, and note that the past is spoken of as what lies before us.

Failing memory is why novelty seems possible. Charles Ellicott states it plainly: what appears new appears so only because its earlier occurrence has been forgotten. Gill lays the fault on both sides: memories fail for what happened within a man’s own lifetime, and for earlier ages men lack history, or have a false one, or one so deficient that very few of the things that were are handed on. Clarke agrees that multitudes of ancient transactions were lost for want of recording, and of many recorded the records are lost—whence men not much acquainted with books suppose things their own discoveries which were printed before they were born. John Wesley treats the verse as answering an objection, that there are inventions unknown to former ages: it rests only on our ignorance of those ages, and since thousands of remarkable actions of our own time will never enter any record, it is reasonable to believe the same of what went before.

At the self-introduction the method changes. Gill and Ellicott mark the turn from general proof to particular instances, beginning with wisdom as the likeliest candidate for happiness, and both note the fitness of the witness, who had every advantage for obtaining it, so that what he concludes may be taken as settled. Wesley itemises the qualifications—a preacher, implying eminent knowledge; a king, with every opportunity of consulting books and men; and king over a wise and happy people, seated where the house of God stood, with its learned priests and its assemblies of wise men. Matthew Henry adds that the court could be made the centre of learning and rendezvous of learned men, since in knowledge as in trade all the profit is by barter and exchange, and describes the study: philosophy and mathematics, husbandry and trade, mechanics, the history of former ages and the state of other kingdoms—a prince made a drudge to learning, not discouraged by its knots nor stopping short of its depths, and doing it not to gratify his genius but to try how far knowledge would settle the mind.

The past tense of was king divides them. Henry hears humility in it: he does not say he is king but that he was, worldly honours being transitory. Clarke calls the verse strange and admitting no easy solution. He canvasses the theory placing the book long after the king among an Israel in another city, the conjecture that it was a posthumous publication in which the departed king still preaches, and the reading that makes the past tense a confession by one no longer worthy of the name—of which last he fears it is not solid. Keil and Delitzsch will have neither complaint nor humility but plain historical statement, rendering it I have been rather than I was, and hold it is the king revived by the book’s author, looking back on his reign; they add that the undivided Israel named in it points before the division, since a king of the smaller kingdom would not so describe himself. Ellicott notes only that the earlier books usually put the title the other way.
13:
Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two verbs of the search. They are not two degrees of one act but two kinds: the first penetrates in depth, investigating an object already in hand, the second goes out in extent, holding a survey to bring what is unknown within the sphere of knowledge. Charles Ellicott explains the idiom of giving the heart, since among the Hebrews the heart is the seat not merely of the feelings but of the intellect, so that it means applying the mind. The word for travail, he adds, occurs nowhere else in the older scriptures. John Gill and John Wesley stress the seriousness of the resolve—a fixed purpose, a determination not to be discouraged, no contentment with superficial knowledge but penetration into the most abstruse learning. Adam Clarke adds how the wisdom was got: he had no intuitive knowledge from God but a capacity to obtain every kind useful to man, laborious discussions and perplexing experiments being how knowledge is got, God having determined it shall be got no other way. Wesley takes the sore travail differently, as a just punishment inflicted on man for eating of the tree of knowledge.

On the verdict, Keil and Delitzsch stress that the seeing was in no way superficial, and that what it found was the fleeting and fruitless nature of human action: no reality in it, no actual consequence, no real issue. Clarke concedes that even where results were most successful he found only rational satisfaction, not the supreme good by which alone the soul is made happy, and quotes a Latin satirist on how anxious our cares and how vain the bent of our desires. Wesley says the vanity is not merely unsatisfying but a breaking of the spirit. Ellicott doubts the familiar rendering vexation of spirit can be justified: nearly the same phrase elsewhere is translated feeding on wind, the word for spirit primarily denoting breath, and many take it so here; but the root meaning to feast on a thing has a secondary sense of delighting in it, and the corresponding Chaldee word means pleasure or will, on which ground the Greek version and many moderns render it effort after wind.

The proverb about the crooked draws the sharpest division. Keil and Delitzsch report the reading that takes the crooked and the wanting of the divine ordering of the world, so that man can neither alter what is unjust in it nor supply what it lacks, and reject it: the context is only labour under the sun and the research directed to it, which brings irregularities to consciousness—some appointed by God, most owing to men’s transgressions—and leaves the observer only lamentation. They gloss the second clause by the maxim that where there is nothing, nothing more is to be counted. Gill takes it morally: whatever a man finds fault with in the works of God he cannot mend, and the crookedness sin has put into men’s hearts is never corrected by natural wisdom, the wisest philosophers with all their parade of learning having effected nothing of the kind, since it is done only by the Spirit and grace of God. Wesley reads it of knowledge itself, which discovers our miseries without removing them, and turns the second clause on the searcher: what is wanting in our knowledge is so much it cannot be numbered, and the more we know the more we see our ignorance. Clarke alone will not let the verse stand as a verdict on nature itself. He grants that a general view shows irregularities we cannot account for and defects that cannot be supplied, but holds that the more we study its operations the more we shall be convinced all is a well-ordered whole, and that in the chain of nature not one link is broken, deficient or lost. Ellicott notes only that both key words are peculiar to this book.
16:
The self-examination is a reckoning. John Gill has him looking into his heart to consider what stock of knowledge he had after all his researches. Adam Clarke supplies the motive: successful in his researches but not happy in his soul, though easy in his circumstances, he entered his own heart and enquired the cause of his discontent. Clarke tallies four attainments—wisdom beyond all men, wealth and honours beyond any other, practical wisdom beyond his predecessors, pleasure carried to its extremes—and finds that none, nor all conjoined, could satisfy the soul, since the soul was made for God and finds happiness in him alone. John Wesley divides the wisdom into what was infused by God and what was improved by study and experience, and takes the comparison to cover governors, priests and private persons alike in the city then most eminent for wisdom. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the expression is involved, the speaker telling his heart what it had experienced, and that the emphatic pronoun is one a king may fairly use.

The pairing of madness and folly with wisdom unsettles everyone. Charles Ellicott says they are not words we expect here, and reports that some have tried by changes of reading to substitute terms of the same kind; taking the text as it stands, he makes the sense a knowing of wisdom through its contraries. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same emendations, one proposing to be rid of the two words and another to read after the Greek, and answer that the text can stand, the aim being clarity about wisdom’s worth against its opposites. Clarke goes furthest. The Greek gives parables and science, he notes, and an older English version error and foolishness, before he offers his own: perhaps gaiety and sobriety are the better meaning for these two difficult words, since he can scarcely think they carry the bad sense our translation gives them—paraphrasing it as trying pleasure in all its forms, and sobriety and self-denial to their utmost. Wesley keeps the plain reading, that the object was to understand the difference of truth and error, of virtue and vice; Gill notes only that the clause is repeated to show how assiduous the search was.

The last verse is given several different griefs. Gill finds it both in getting wisdom and in losing it once gotten, and glosses the word as indignation, at himself and others, a man being more sensible of the follies and weakness of human nature. Ellicott renders it simply irritation. Keil and Delitzsch insist the two words cover mental as well as bodily suffering, and set aside the proverb that wisdom causes headache; they quote a philosopher’s remark that a true knowledge of good and evil is often not enough to restrain the desires, so that a man aware of his weakness must confess he sees and approves the better course and follows the worse. Their own account is that knowledge always carries the shadow of sorrowful consciousness: the wise man gains insight into the thousandfold woes of the natural and human world, which reflects itself in him without his being able to change it, so that the more forms of evil he observes, the greater the heart-sorrow his useless knowledge occasions. Clarke says the more we know of ourselves the less satisfied we are with our hearts, and the more we know of mankind the less willing to trust it, since apart from God the principal objects of knowledge are natural and moral evils. Wesley’s list is longest: the labour consumes the spirits and shortens life; the learner is deceived by knowledge falsely so called and perplexed with doubts ignorant men never feel; he sees his own infirmities more clearly and how little his knowledge removes them; what he has only increases his thirst; and it dies with him, leaving him no better, and possibly worse, than the most unlearned man alive.
